title: How the Story Ends
subtitle: A five-session study on the last things, holding open hands on the timeline and a closed fist on the center.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of being handed a chart and told it is the gospel. It is for the believer who has watched a date come and go, who has seen a church split over the rapture, who has read Revelation and felt more confused than comforted, and who suspects there is more here than a code to be cracked. It walks slowly through five movements on the end of the story, on how to read apocalyptic literature without turning it into a newspaper, on the three readings of the thousand years, on the rapture and the dispensational debate, on the already and the not yet that every serious Christian shares, and on the new creation that is the actual hope, the world made right rather than abandoned.

The editorial rule of this study is one thing, held without apology. Every major view of the end gets stated by its best advocate, in its strongest form, before anyone is allowed to argue against it. Premillennialism, postmillennialism, and amillennialism each get their best scholars and their strongest scriptural case. The dispensational rapture gets Darby and Scofield and Blaising at full strength before the alternatives answer. This is not a study that sells you one timeline as the answer and pretends the others are for the unserious. It refuses that, because faithful, careful, Bible-loving Christians have landed in all three camps for two thousand years, and a study that flattens them into one is lying to you about the church.

What the study will not compromise is the center, and the leader must guard it. Christ has come. Christ will come again. The dead will be raised. The world will be made right. On that, there is no open hand. The timeline is where the room is free to disagree. The creed is where it is not. And the writer stands inside all of it, because Bell came to faith from atheism arguing that the whole thing was a fairy tale for people afraid to die, and he has done his own date-math in the dark, and he has used the end times as an escape from a world he was supposed to love. He does not write from above this. He writes from inside it. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: Reading the End Rightly
sessions.aim: To learn what kind of writing Revelation and Daniel actually are before deciding what they mean, and to clear the ground of a long, sobering record of confident predictions that were confidently wrong.
sessions.summary: A man once told Bell, with total certainty, that the European Union was the revived Roman Empire of Daniel and that the end would arrive within five years. That was a long time ago, and the man is still waiting. The first question of any study of the last things is not when. It is how do we read this. Apocalyptic literature is a genre, a way of writing born among a persecuted people, dense with symbol and number and beast and throne, and it does not work like a history textbook or a coded calendar. Bell takes the strong form of the literalist instinct, that if the Bible says a thousand years it means a thousand years, that to spiritualize the text is to evade it, and he grants the real fear underneath it, the fear that symbolic reading is just a way of making the Bible say whatever you want. He grants the danger. Then he turns it. Revelation was written to seven actual churches under an actual empire, and they did not read it as a prediction about helicopters or the Soviet Union. They read it as a vision that the slaughtered Lamb sits on the throne and Rome does not, and that vision steadied them to die rather than burn incense to Caesar. Read the end rightly and it does not feed your speculation. It steels your faith. Then the sobering record. From the Montanists to William Miller to the chart-makers of the last century, the church has a long history of setting dates and being wrong, every single time, and that record is not a footnote. It is a warning the study takes to heart from the first night.

keyScripture.why: John opens by calling the book a revelation given to show the servants of Christ what must soon take place, and pronounces a blessing on the one who reads and keeps it, framing the whole book as a word to be heard and obeyed by its first readers, not a cipher to be decoded by a later generation.

discussion.q: Before tonight, where did most of your ideas about the end times actually come from, a sermon, a novel, a chart, a movie, or the text of Scripture itself?
discussion.behind: Surface the source before touching the doctrine. Most people in the room learned their eschatology from culture rather than from study, and naming that gently lowers the defensiveness. The point is not to embarrass anyone but to expose how much we assume we got from the Bible and did not. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Revelation was first read aloud to seven real churches under Roman pressure. What changes when you picture them hearing it as people about to be asked to worship Caesar, rather than as a code about our future?
discussion.behind: Move the room from decoding to listening. The aim is to relocate the book to its first hearers, who needed courage and not a calendar. Help them feel that the original purpose was to steady the persecuted, which reframes how we should read it now.

discussion.q: Bell takes the literalist instinct seriously, that a thousand years should mean a thousand years and that spiritualizing the text can be a dodge. What is true in that worry, and where can it go wrong?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness from the start. The literalist fear is legitimate, symbolic reading can be abused to mean anything. But apocalyptic genre uses number and image symbolically by design. Help the room hold both, that the text must constrain us and that the genre is not a newspaper.

discussion.q: The church has set dates and been wrong every single time, for two thousand years. Why do you think the impulse to predict keeps coming back, even after that record?
discussion.behind: Get underneath the appeal. Date-setting offers control, certainty, and the thrill of being the ones who know. The aim is honest recognition that the impulse is in all of us, a way of mastering a future only God holds. Keep it self-implicating, not mocking of the predictors.

discussion.q: Bell admits he once used end-times speculation to feel like an insider, one of the few who really understood. Where have you felt the pull of secret knowledge about the future, and what does that pull reveal?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication. The hunger to know the end is often the hunger to be special, to possess what others lack. You are not shaming the curious. You want each person, the leader first, to see the pride that can hide inside prophecy study. Go first.

objections.objection: If you do not read Revelation literally, you can make it mean anything you want. The plain words are there for a reason, and spiritualizing the text is just a polite way of refusing to believe what it says.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because it is a real danger. Symbolic reading can absolutely be abused, stretched until the text means whatever the reader already wanted, and a great deal of bad teaching does exactly that. The text must constrain us. Then make the distinction with care. Reading apocalyptic according to its genre is not the same as making it say anything. When Revelation calls Jesus a Lamb, no one thinks he is a literal sheep, and when it shows a dragon with seven heads, no one is scanning the zoo. The book announces its own symbolic method from the first verse, where it says it signifies its message. To read a beast as an empire is not to evade the text. It is to read it the way its first hearers, steeped in Daniel and Ezekiel, were equipped to read it. The discipline is to let the symbol mean what the wider Scripture and the original setting say it means, which constrains the reader far more tightly than the literalist fears.

objections.objection: All this talk about genre and original readers is just modern scholarship explaining away the supernatural. The simple believer reads the words and trusts them. The professors read the words and water them down.
objections.response: Grant what is right, because there is something to guard here. Scholarship can curdle into a sophistication that no longer believes anything supernatural at all, and a faith that needs a seminary degree to read its own Bible has lost something Jesus blessed in the little children. Honor the plain believer. Then press the other edge gently. Taking the genre seriously is not watering down the supernatural, it is taking the inspired author seriously enough to read what he actually wrote in the form he actually chose. God gave us poetry as poetry, history as history, parable as parable, and apocalypse as apocalypse, and to read a vision as if it were a wire-service report is not more faithful, it is less. The most reverent thing you can do with a text is to read it as the kind of thing it is. That is not less belief. It is belief that does its homework.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What have you secretly hoped to gain by knowing how the world ends, certainty, control, the feeling of being one of the few who really understands?
sessions.practice: This week, read Revelation chapters 1 through 3 in one sitting, slowly, as a letter to seven frightened churches rather than as a puzzle about the future. Do not try to decode anything. Just notice what the risen Christ says to ordinary congregations under pressure, what he praises and what he warns. Write down one thing he says to those churches that you needed to hear yourself.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you gave us the visions not to make us clever but to make us faithful, and we have turned them into puzzles and charts and a way of feeling special. Forgive us the pride that hides inside our certainty about the future. Teach us to read your word as the kind of thing it is, to hear what the slaughtered Lamb said to the trembling churches, and to be steadied for our own day rather than distracted from it. You hold the times in your hand. Help us to trust the hand and stop grabbing for the calendar. Amen.
reflection: Where did my picture of the end times really come from, and have I ever checked it against the text rather than against the culture that gave it to me?
Have I treated Revelation as a code to be cracked rather than a word to be obeyed, and what would change if I read it the way its first hearers did?
What is the pull of secret knowledge about the future for me, and what does that pull reveal about what I am really after?
sessions.teaching: Start where Bell starts, with a man who knew. He told Bell, with total and untroubled certainty, that the European Union was the revived Roman Empire predicted in Daniel, that the pieces were all in place, and that the end would arrive inside of five years. That conversation happened a long time ago. The man is, as far as anyone knows, still here, still waiting, and probably still certain, having simply moved the date. He is not a fool. He is part of a very long line, and the line is the first thing a study of the last things has to reckon with honestly. So we do not begin with when. We begin with the harder and more important question, the one almost no one asks before they start drawing arrows on a timeline. How do we read this. What kind of writing is Revelation, what kind of writing is Daniel, and what did God intend us to do with it. Until we answer that, every conclusion we reach will be built on sand. Here is what gets missed. Apocalyptic is a genre. It is a recognizable way of writing, with its own conventions, that flourished among the people of God in seasons of crushing pressure, and it is dense by design with symbol, with number, with beast and horn and throne and lampstand and a great red dragon. It does not work the way a history textbook works, and it does not work the way a coded calendar works. To read it as either is to misread it at the root. Now take the literalist instinct at its strongest, because it deserves respect and not a sneer. The instinct says this. If God says a thousand years, God means a thousand years, and the moment you start calling the numbers symbolic you have handed yourself a license to make the text mean anything you please. There is a real fear under that, and it is a good fear. Symbolic reading can be abused. It has been abused, stretched and twisted until the Bible becomes a mirror for whatever the reader already believed. Grant all of it. The text must constrain the reader, or we are not reading the text at all, we are using it. But here is the turn, and it matters. Reading according to genre is the opposite of reading without constraint. When John shows us Jesus as a Lamb standing as though slain, no one in the room thinks the Savior is livestock. When he shows us a beast rising from the sea with seven heads and ten horns, the first hearers did not reach for a bestiary, they reached for Daniel, where beasts are empires, because they had been trained by their own Scriptures to read the image. The symbol is not a blank check. The symbol has a meaning fixed by the wider Bible and by the world the book was written into, and that meaning constrains the careful reader far more tightly than wooden literalism ever could. So who were they, these first readers. Revelation names them. Seven churches in Asia Minor, real congregations in real cities under a real empire, and the pressure on them was specific and deadly. They were being asked, increasingly, to acknowledge Caesar as lord, to drop a pinch of incense on the imperial altar, to call the empire eternal and divine. And into that pressure John sends a vision, and the vision is not a prediction about the Soviet Union or barcodes or attack helicopters. The vision is this. The slaughtered Lamb is on the throne. Rome is not eternal. The beast that looks invincible is already judged. The blood of the martyrs is not wasted. Worship the Lamb and not the empire, and though it cost you everything, you are on the winning side of history. That vision did something. It steadied frightened people to face lions rather than burn the incense. Read the end rightly and that is what it does. It does not feed your speculation about the date. It steels your faith for the cost of following Jesus now. And then there is the record, which we have to face squarely, because it is not a footnote, it is a warning written in two thousand years of disappointment. The Montanists in the second century expected the New Jerusalem to descend in Phrygia. It did not. William Miller calculated the return of Christ for 1844, and gathered tens of thousands of sober, decent people who gave away their goods and waited on hillsides for a Savior who did not come, and the day passed into what they themselves called the Great Disappointment, a grief so heavy it broke some of their faith outright. The last century produced a small industry of charts and best-selling books pinning the end to the day's headlines, matching beasts to dictators and the mark to whatever new technology had just appeared, and the events kept moving and the end kept not coming and the charts were quietly redrawn for the next generation of buyers. Every confident date, without exception, has been wrong, and not once has the failure made the next predictor more cautious. And I have to stand inside this, because I have felt the pull. As a younger believer I loved the feeling of being an insider, one of the few who had cracked the code, who could read the newspaper with the Bible open and see what the ordinary Christians missed. That was not faith. That was pride wearing the costume of prophecy, and Jesus said plainly that not even the Son knew the day or the hour, which should have ended my certainty and did not, for far too long. So here is the verdict for this first night, and the leader must hold it cleanly. We are not here to set a date, because the One we follow refused to, and everyone who has ignored him has been embarrassed by history. We are here to learn to read the kind of writing this is, to hear it the way the dying churches heard it, and to let it do to us what it did to them. Not speculation. Steel. We clear the ground tonight so that we can build something true on it.

scriptureStudy.note: The book opens by calling itself a revelation that signifies its message, language that announces a symbolic method from the first verse, and it blesses the one who reads and keeps it, framing the whole as a word to obey, not a code to crack.

Daniel sees four great beasts rising from the sea, and the text itself later identifies them as kingdoms. Here is the school the first readers of Revelation attended. Beasts are empires, and they learned to read the image long before John wrote.

In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed. The arc of Daniel is the rise and fall of empires under a God who outlasts them all, which is the same comfort Revelation later presses.

Concerning that day or hour no one knows, not even the angels, nor the Son, but only the Father. Jesus places the date beyond his own earthly knowing, which should end every chart and humble every predictor.

It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. The risen Christ redirects the disciples from the timetable to the mission, telling them to be witnesses rather than calculators.

With the Lord one day is as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day. Peter warns against reading God's clock by ours, and grounds the apparent delay not in absence but in patience that wants more to be saved.

This calls for wisdom, let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast. Even the most famous number in the book is offered to the first readers as a riddle pointing at a present power, not a code for a future microchip.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the history of apocalyptic as a form, because Revelation did not drop out of the sky into a vacuum, and reading it well means knowing the tradition it belongs to. Between the testaments and into the first century, a whole body of Jewish apocalyptic writing developed among a people living under one empire after another, from the Babylonians to the Greeks to the Romans, and it shared a recognizable toolkit, visions and angelic interpreters, cosmic symbols, beasts standing for kingdoms, numbers carrying meaning rather than arithmetic, and a fierce insistence that despite all appearances God reigns and the oppressor will fall. Daniel sits at the headwaters of this stream, and Revelation flows from it, soaked in the imagery of Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, and Isaiah, so that a reader who does not know those books will inevitably misread John. Set this beside the modern habit, especially strong in the last two centuries, of reading Revelation as if it were composed for the twenty-first-century newspaper reader, its symbols matched to current headlines, and ask what is lost when a book written to comfort the persecuted is repurposed to thrill the comfortable. A serious group should weigh both the gain and the danger here. The gain of historical reading is that the book finally makes sense as what it is, a pastoral and prophetic word to suffering saints. The danger to guard against is the opposite error, treating it as merely a first-century document with nothing to say to us, when in fact the same Lamb still reigns and the same call to faithful endurance still stands. The discipline is to read Revelation first to its own churches, and only then, carefully, to ours, never skipping the first step on the way to the second.
sessions.caseStudy: Consider the Millerites, because their story is the whole first session in miniature, and it is not ancient. In the 1830s and 1840s, a Baptist preacher named William Miller, an earnest and sincere man, worked out from the prophecies of Daniel that Christ would return around 1843, later refined to October 22, 1844. He was not a crank on the fringe. He drew tens of thousands of followers across the American Northeast, careful Bible readers, decent people, who believed the calculation because the math looked sound and the verses were right there. Some sold their farms. Some left crops unharvested, reasoning there would be no winter to feed. They gathered, they waited, and the day came and the day went, and Christ did not return, and they called what followed, in their own words, the Great Disappointment. Now resist the easy mockery, because that is the point of the case. These were not stupid or faithless people. They were serious students of the same Bible we are holding, undone by the same impulse that is in every one of us, the hunger to know the date, to master the future, to be the ones who saw it coming. Ask the group the uncomfortable question. What did Miller do wrong, exactly. Not that he loved the return of Christ, which is right and good. He confused the genre and ignored the plain word of Jesus that no one knows the day. The Millerites are not a cautionary tale about other people. They are a mirror, and the wise group looks into it.
