sessions.title: The New Creation
sessions.aim: To recover the actual Christian hope, the resurrection of the body and the renewal of heaven and earth, the world made right rather than abandoned, and to end the study with weight rather than a tidy chart, at the edge of a hope that is not escape.
sessions.summary: The study ends where the Bible ends, and it is not where most Christians think. Ask the average believer what the Christian hope is and you will hear about souls going up to heaven when they die, leaving the body and the earth behind forever. The New Testament says something larger and stranger and far more physical. The hope is resurrection, the body raised, and new creation, heaven coming down to earth, the two joined, the world not discarded but renewed. N.T. Wright has spent a career recovering this, that the goal is not us going up to heaven but heaven coming down, the new Jerusalem descending, God dwelling with his people on a renewed earth. Bell takes the strong form of the spiritualized hope, that what matters is the soul's eternal communion with God and the physical is secondary, and he grants what it gets right, that to be with Christ is the heart of it and that the soul does go to be with him at death. Then he turns it. The Bible's final image is not disembodied souls in a cloud but a city, a feast, a healed creation, resurrected bodies, every tear wiped away, death itself dead. This hope is not escape from the world but the redemption of it, and that changes everything about how we live now, because a world destined for renewal is a world worth loving and tending now. The study does not resolve into a chart. It ends at the edge of a hope too large to diagram, the dead raised, the world made right, God with us, and it leaves the weight of that on the room.

keyScripture.why: John's final vision is not of souls ascending to heaven but of the new Jerusalem descending to earth, God coming to dwell with his people, every tear wiped away and death itself abolished, which corrects the popular picture of the Christian hope and gives the study its true ending.

discussion.q: If someone asked you what the Christian hope is, what would you have said before tonight, and how close was it to souls floating up to heaven forever?
discussion.behind: Surface the popular picture honestly. Most of the room carries a half-pagan image of disembodied bliss in the clouds. The aim is to expose the gap between that and the Bible's bodily, earthly, renewed-creation hope, without shaming anyone for the picture they inherited.

discussion.q: John's final vision is the new Jerusalem coming down to earth, not us going up to heaven. Why does the direction matter, and what changes when heaven comes to us rather than us escaping to it?
discussion.behind: Land Wright's central correction. The aim is for the room to feel the difference between escape and renewal, between abandoning the world and the world being healed. Help them see that the descent of the city means the material world has a future, not just our souls.

discussion.q: The creed says we believe in the resurrection of the body, not the immortality of the soul alone. Why do you think the church insisted on bodies, and what does it say about how God feels about the physical world?
discussion.behind: Press on the scandal of resurrection. The aim is to recover the goodness of the body and the material creation in God's purposes. Many are surprised the hope is bodily at all. Help them see God affirming, not discarding, what he made.

discussion.q: If the world is going to be renewed rather than destroyed, how does that change the worth of ordinary work, beauty, justice, and care for creation done now?
discussion.behind: Connect the hope to the present, tying back to session four. The aim is to see that a renewed-creation hope dignifies present labor, that what we do in the body and in the world is not erased. Press for concrete implications, not sentiment.

discussion.q: This study ends without a chart, on purpose, at the edge of a hope too large to diagram. What is it you most long to see made right when Christ returns, and what does that longing tell you?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study with weight and self-implication. Do not resolve it. Invite each person, the leader first, to name the brokenness they ache to see healed, the grave they want emptied. End at the edge of hope, carrying the longing, not tying a bow. Go first.

objections.objection: The real hope is spiritual, the soul with God forever. All this talk about renewed earth and resurrected bodies is too earthy. Heaven is about being with God, and the physical world and the body are just the temporary shell we finally leave behind.
objections.response: Grant the precious truth in this, because the heart of it is right and must not be lost. To be with Christ is indeed the center of the hope, far better, as Paul says, and at death the believer does go to be with the Lord, consciously and joyfully, which is a real comfort for the grieving and must never be denied. Honor that fully. Then turn it with the whole weight of Scripture, because the spiritualized hope stops too soon. The being-with-Christ at death, glorious as it is, is not the final state, it is the waiting room. The Bible's final word is not a soul in heaven but a body raised, the dead coming out of the tombs, and not a world abandoned but a world renewed, the new heavens and new earth, the city of God descending. The body is not a shell God means to discard, it is part of what he made and called good and intends to raise, which is why the Son himself rose bodily and ate fish on the shore. To treat the physical as merely temporary is closer to the old Greek contempt for matter than to the Hebrew and Christian conviction that creation is good and will be redeemed. The hope is more physical than you feared, not less, and that is better news, not worse.

objections.objection: A renewed earth sounds like wishful thinking, a comforting fairy tale for people who cannot accept that death is the end. The skeptic in the room says this is exactly the pie-in-the-sky religion was always selling, and it is no more believable for being earthy instead of cloudy.
objections.response: Take this seriously and without defensiveness, because Bell himself once made this exact argument as an atheist and means to answer it honestly rather than dismiss it. Yes, a hope this large could be wishful thinking, and the longing for the world to be made right does not by itself prove it will be. Grant the fairness of the suspicion. Then put the actual Christian claim on the table, which is not a vague hope but a specific historical assertion, that one man already rose, bodily, from the dead, as the firstfruits, the first instance of exactly the renewal promised for everything else. The Christian hope is not built on how badly we want death to lose. It is built on a claim that death already lost, once, in a garden outside Jerusalem, and that the empty tomb is the seed of the renewed creation, the down payment on a world made right. You can weigh that claim, examine the evidence for the resurrection, decide whether it holds. But it is not mere wishing. It is a hope anchored to an event, and that is a different kind of thing entirely. The study does not ask you to want it true. It asks you to consider whether it is.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you picture the world finally made right, every tear wiped away and death itself dead, what is the one loss you most long to see undone, and dare you hope it will be?
sessions.practice: This week, read Revelation 21 and 22 slowly, the very end of the Bible, and read it not as a code but as a homecoming. Notice every physical detail, the city, the river, the tree, the healed nations, the absence of tears and death. Then look at the world around you, your own street, your own griefs, and ask what it would mean for this, all of it, to be made right and not thrown away. Write down what longing the reading stirred, and bring that longing to God.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord God, you are not going to abandon the world you made and called good. You are going to make it new, raise the dead, wipe away every tear, and dwell with us on a healed earth, and the grave that has taken those we love will give them back. We have made our hope too small, a flight to a cloud, when you promised a city and a feast and a body raised. Enlarge our hope to the size of your promise. Teach us to love the world you intend to heal, to wait without despair, and to carry our griefs toward the day when death itself will die. We do not know all the order of the end. We know you are coming, and we know you make all things new. Come, Lord Jesus. Amen.
reflection: How small had my hope become, and what would change if I really believed God means to raise my body and renew the whole earth rather than rescue my soul out of it?
If the world is destined for renewal and not the trash heap, what in my life and my work takes on a weight it did not have before?
What loss do I most ache to see undone, and can I let the resurrection of Christ be the ground of daring to hope it will be?
sessions.teaching: We end where the Bible ends, and it is not where most of us were taught to look. Ask the average Christian, even the devout one, what the Christian hope is, what we are finally waiting for, and the answer will almost always be some version of this. When I die, my soul goes up to heaven to be with God forever, leaving this body and this earth behind. That answer is half true and badly incomplete, and the incompleteness has done real damage to how the church lives and hopes and dies. Because the New Testament, when you actually read it to the end, describes something larger and stranger and far more physical than a soul in a cloud. The hope of the Bible is two things the popular picture mostly forgets. Resurrection, and new creation. Take resurrection first. The creeds the church hammered out do not say we believe in the immortality of the soul. The pagan philosophers already believed that. The creeds say we believe in the resurrection of the body, which is a far more scandalous and far more wonderful claim. It says that the body, this physical thing God made and called good, is not a shell to be sloughed off but part of what God intends to redeem and raise. Jesus did not rise as a ghost. He rose with a body that could be touched, that bore the scars, that ate broiled fish on the shore in front of his astonished friends. And Paul calls that resurrection the firstfruits, the first instance of a harvest, which means what happened to Jesus is the pattern and the promise of what will happen to us. Not escape from the body. The redemption of it. Now new creation, and here N.T. Wright has spent a career trying to wake the church up to what it had half forgotten. Look at how the Bible actually ends. Not with the saved souls flying up to heaven. The exact opposite. John sees the new Jerusalem, the city of God, coming down out of heaven to earth, and he hears a great voice announce that the dwelling of God is now with man, that God will dwell with them. The movement is downward, not upward. Heaven comes to earth. The two are joined. The goal of the whole story is not humanity evacuated from a doomed creation to a disembodied paradise elsewhere. The goal is heaven and earth made one, the world we know not deleted but healed, renewed, made finally and fully right. Wright puts it sharply, that the question is not how we get to heaven but how heaven comes here, and that the Christian hope was hijacked somewhere along the way into a Greek dream of escaping matter, when the Hebrew and Christian vision was always the rescue and renewal of matter itself. So take the spiritualized hope at its strongest, because it is sincere and it holds something precious. It says what finally matters is the soul's eternal communion with God, that to be with Christ is the heart of everything, and that the physical is secondary. And it is right about the center. To be with Christ is the heart of it. Paul does say that to depart and be with Christ is far better, and at death the believer truly does go to be consciously, joyfully with the Lord, which is a comfort the grieving must never be denied. Hold that as true. But here is the turn, and it is everything. Being with Christ at death, glorious as it is, is not the final state. It is the intermediate state, the waiting, the in-between, the soul with the Lord while it waits for the day the body will rise. The final word of the Bible is not a soul in heaven. It is the trumpet, the graves opening, the dead raised imperishable, and a new heaven and new earth where God wipes away every tear from every eye and death itself, the last enemy, is finally and forever dead. That is not a smaller hope than souls in heaven. It is an immeasurably larger one, and it is more physical, not less, which is exactly the opposite of what we feared and far better news than we dared. And this changes everything about how we live now, which is why it is the right place to end the whole study. If the world is going to be thrown away, then nothing in it finally matters except getting souls out, and we are back to the escapism we rejected last week. But if the world is going to be renewed, if this creation is destined to be set free from its bondage and made right, then everything you do in the body and in the world takes on a weight that escapism could never give it. The cup of cold water, the work done well, the beauty made, the justice fought for, the broken thing mended, the love poured out, none of it is wasted, none of it is polishing brass on a sinking ship, because the ship is not sinking, it is being remade, and what is done in love now is somehow taken up into the world that is coming. I came to faith out of atheism, and the argument I used to make, the one I made loudest, was that all of this was a fairy tale, a story frightened people told because they could not bear that death was the end. And I will not pretend that suspicion is foolish, because a hope this large could be wishful thinking, the longing does not prove the thing. But here is what stopped me, and it is where I will leave you. The Christian hope is not finally built on how badly we want death to lose. It is built on the claim that death already lost, once, in a garden outside Jerusalem, that a real man was really dead and really rose, the firstfruits, the first piece of the new creation breaking into the old. If that happened, then the rest of it, the raised bodies and the healed earth and the city coming down and the tears wiped away, is not wishing. It is the inevitable harvest of a seed already planted. So I am not going to end this study with a chart. I refuse to, because the hope is too large to diagram and the diagramming was always a way of mastering what we were meant to long for. I am going to end it at the edge, where the Bible ends, with the dead coming out of the tombs, and the world we love made right instead of thrown away, and God himself come down to dwell with us, and every grave we have wept over giving back what it took. We do not know all the order of the end, and we have spent five sessions being honest about that. But we know this, and on this there is no open hand. Christ has come. Christ will come again. The dead will be raised. And the world will be made right. Carry that out of this room. It is heavier than any chart, and it is the only hope big enough to live and die on.

scriptureStudy.note: A new heaven and a new earth, the holy city coming down out of heaven, God dwelling with his people, every tear wiped away and death no more. The movement is heaven descending to a renewed earth, not souls escaping upward, the Bible's true picture of the end.
Behold, I am making all things new. Not making all new things, but making all things new, the renewal of what already exists rather than its replacement, the world redeemed and not discarded.

Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. His bodily resurrection is the first instance and the guarantee of ours, the seed of the new creation already sprung up in the middle of the old world.

The body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown a natural body and raised a spiritual body. The resurrection body is real and physical, transformed and glorified, continuous with this body yet free from death, not a discarding of the body but its redemption.

The creation waits with eager longing to be set free from its bondage to decay and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. The creation itself, not only souls, is the object of redemption, destined for liberation and not the trash heap.

We await a Savior who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body. The hope is explicitly bodily, our humble bodies made like the resurrected body of Christ, which corrects any picture of a purely spiritual destiny.

The river of life, the tree of life with leaves for the healing of the nations, and no more night, for the Lord God will be their light. The very end of the Bible is a healed and flourishing creation, physical and abundant, God dwelling with his people forever.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long struggle between two views of the body and the material world, because the recovery of the Bible's new-creation hope is, in large part, the recovery of a Hebrew conviction against a Greek one that infiltrated the church early and never fully left. The Greek philosophical tradition, in its dominant strands, treated matter as lower than spirit and often as the prison of the soul, so that salvation meant the soul's release from the body and the material world, an escape upward into pure spirit. Much popular Christianity quietly absorbed this, until heaven became a disembodied elsewhere and the resurrection of the body, though confessed in the creed every Sunday, was functionally forgotten in favor of going to heaven when we die. Against this, the Hebrew Scriptures and the New Testament insist relentlessly that God made matter and called it good, that the body is not a prison but a gift, that the Word became flesh and rose in flesh, and that the destiny of the redeemed is not flight from creation but the renewal of creation with resurrected bodies to inhabit it. A serious group should weigh how deeply the Greek picture still shapes funeral talk, hymn lyrics, and private imagination, and how much hope is lost when the resurrection is traded for a soul in the clouds. The discipline is to let the full biblical hope reshape the imagination, to grieve and to die as people who believe not merely that the soul survives but that the body will rise and the earth will be healed, and to let that larger hope reach back into how we treat the body, the creation, and the ordinary material life we are living now, none of which God intends to throw away.
sessions.caseStudy: Sit with a graveside, because this is where the doctrine of the new creation either becomes real or stays an abstraction. A family buries a young mother, far too soon, and at the service two kinds of comfort are offered. The first, well-meant and common, says she is in a better place now, she is an angel watching over you, her soul is free of the body at last and at peace in heaven, and there is real truth in part of it, she is with Christ, which is far better. But notice what that comfort quietly concedes. It treats the body in the ground as the discarded part, the shell, the thing that does not matter, and it leaves the grave itself as the final fact about her flesh. The second comfort, the fuller one the Bible actually gives, says something the first does not dare. It says that the body in that ground is not garbage, that it is precious, that it is a seed, and that the same God who raised Jesus bodily will raise her, that this grave is not the end of her body but its waiting place, and that there is coming a morning when death gives back everything it has ever taken. Ask the group which comfort they have heard at funerals, and which one they would want spoken over their own grave. The case makes the session unavoidably personal, because every one of them will stand at such a graveside, and most will stand in such a grave, and the size of the hope they carry there is the whole point of the study.

memoryVerse.text: And he who was seated on the throne said, behold, I am making all things new.

leaderPrimer: You said yes to leading this, and before you open the first session you need to know exactly what you are holding, because this study is built differently from most, and the difference is the whole point. This is a study about the end times, the last things, and you already know that almost nothing in the Christian life produces more heat, more division, more confident shouting, and more broken fellowship than this topic. So hear the aim plainly. This study is not here to tell your group which view of the end is correct. It is here to teach them to hold the question rightly, with open hands on the timeline and a closed fist on the center. Say that phrase to yourself until it is yours, because you are going to need it. Open hands on the timeline. Closed fist on the center. The single most important thing I can tell you, and I want it as plain as I know how to make it, is this. Faithful, Bible-loving, serious Christians have disagreed about the order and shape of the end for two thousand years, and they still do, and this disagreement is not a test of who really belongs to Christ. The early church did not put the millennium in the creeds. It did not make the rapture a mark of true faith. It confessed that Christ has come, that he will come again to judge the living and the dead, that the dead will be raised, and that the world will be made right, and on the rest it left room. You must do the same. If your group leaves this study more divided over the timeline than when it began, more suspicious of one another, more certain that the people in the other camp are unserious or unfaithful, then the study failed, however much Scripture got quoted along the way. Guard against that with everything in you, because it is the specific danger of this particular subject, and it is real. Now understand the editorial rule that shapes every session, because you have to defend it actively. The rule is equal-weight steelmans. That means every major view gets stated by its best advocate, in its strongest form, before anyone is allowed to argue against it. The sessions are written this way on purpose. Session two states premillennialism, postmillennialism, and amillennialism each at full strength before any critique. Session three states the dispensational rapture at full strength, by Darby and Scofield and Blaising, before the alternatives answer. This is not a debate format where your favorite view wins on points. It is a discipline of honoring the people who read the same Bible and landed elsewhere, and your job as leader is to enforce it in the room. When someone in your group rushes to attack a view before it has been fairly stated, slow them down. Ask them first to state that view so well that someone who holds it would nod. Do not let the room knock down straw men. The test of whether your group has understood a view is whether they can argue for it, not against it. If you cannot do this yourself, if you walk in already certain that one view is the faithful one and the others are errors to be corrected, you will poison the whole thing, so deal with your own heart first. You almost certainly have a view. Most leaders do, and that is fine. But you are not here to recruit. If a member asks you privately where you land, you may tell them, gently, as one reading among several, and then you must turn them straight back to the text and the other views. In the room, keep your own conviction quiet enough that no one feels the pressure to agree with the leader to belong. The fastest way to break this study is for the group to figure out which side the facilitator is on and to start performing agreement. Know the people who will be in your room, because this topic draws specific kinds. The first is the certain one, often raised on one system, usually the dispensational rapture, who has never been told the other views exist and may be genuinely shaken to learn that Augustine and Calvin read it differently. Handle this person with patience, not triumph. The goal is not to demolish their view but to widen their sense of who counts as faithful, and that takes time and gentleness, not a clever argument that humiliates them. The second is the burned one, who grew up on charts and date-predictions that failed, watched a teacher set a date that came and went, and walked away from the whole subject in disgust or quiet embarrassment. This person needs to discover that there is a serious, humble, non-crazy way to hold the Christian hope, and your steadiness will matter more to them than any single point. The third is the curious skeptic, maybe not yet a believer, who finds the whole thing either ridiculous or fascinating, and who is watching to see whether Christians can talk about this without losing their minds or their charity. Bell came to faith from exactly that posture, an atheist who thought the end times was a fairy tale for the frightened, so the study is written with that person partly in view, and your honesty and humility will preach to them louder than certainty ever could. The fourth is the divider, the one who genuinely believes their timeline is a matter of orthodoxy and wants to make it a boundary. Love this person, and do not let them run the room. When they try to make the millennium a test of faith, return gently and firmly to the center, to what the creed actually says, and to the two thousand years of faithful disagreement. Now the part it would be easiest to skip, your own heart, because you cannot lead people to humility you do not have. Bell does not write this from above the fray, as the calm expert who has the end figured out. He came to faith out of atheism, and the argument he made loudest as an unbeliever was that the whole Christian hope was wishful thinking, a story for people too afraid to face that death is the end. He has done his own date-math in the dark, felt the pull of secret knowledge, the thrill of being the one who cracked the code. He has used the rapture as an escape hatch, a way of not loving a world he expected to flee. He stands inside every distortion this study names, and the power of the thing depends on you standing there too. So before session one, find your own version of it. Maybe you are the certain one who needs to discover the other views are held by saints. Maybe you are the burned one still embarrassed by a failed prediction. Maybe you secretly suspect the skeptic has a point. Whatever it is, name it honestly, and let your honesty be the permission that frees the room to be honest too. A leader who says I used to be sure and I have learned to hold this more humbly can lead this study. A leader who walks in with the answers will turn it into the very thing it exists to prevent. One practical word on the shape of each session. The teaching sections are long and they are meant to be, because steelmanning takes room, and you should read them ahead of time so you can summarize fairly rather than reading them aloud cold. The discussion questions carry the answer behind them, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer, so you are not improvising. When the room gets heated over a point of timeline, and it will, do not let the heat run. Slow your own voice, return to the center, remind them what they share, and move toward the prayer, because this lands not as a debate won but as a hope carried. And here is your charge. You are not the referee who declares a winning view, and you are certainly not the recruiter for your own. You are the guardian of two things at once, the freedom to disagree about the timeline and the refusal to disagree about the center. Hold both. Make the room a place where a dispensationalist and an amillennialist can sit at the same table, state each other's views with respect, and walk out more convinced than ever that Christ has come and is coming again, and more charitable than ever toward the brother who reads Revelation 20 differently. Refuse every attempt to turn a contested timeline into a test of faith. Keep the center bright and the secondary questions open. End every session at the edge of the hope and not in the middle of an argument, because the point was never to settle the chart. The point was to make a room full of people, you first, who hold the Christian hope with both conviction and humility, who long for the King who is coming, and who have stopped using the end of the world as a weapon against each other. Go humbly. Go honestly. Go first.

faq.q: Does this study tell me which view of the end times is the right one?
faq.a: No, and that refusal is deliberate, not a dodge. The study presents the three major readings of the millennium, premillennial, postmillennial, and amillennial, and the dispensational rapture debate, each stated by its best advocate at full strength before any critique, because faithful, Bible-loving Christians have landed in all of them for two thousand years. The aim is to teach you to hold the question rightly, with open hands on the timeline and a closed fist on the center, rather than to recruit you to one camp. The study does insist, without compromise, on what the whole church confesses, that Christ has come, that he will come again to judge the living and the dead, that the dead will be raised, and that the world will be made right. Where the creed is firm, the study is firm. Where the creed left room, the study leaves room, and it asks you to do the same.

faq.q: What does it mean that the study uses equal-weight steelmans?
faq.a: A steelman is the opposite of a straw man. Instead of stating a view in its weakest, most attackable form so it is easy to knock down, you state it in its strongest, most persuasive form, the way its best defender would put it, before you offer any criticism. Equal-weight means every major view gets that same fair treatment, none of them set up to lose. So in this study, premillennialism, postmillennialism, and amillennialism each get their best scholars and their strongest scriptural case stated fully and fairly before anyone argues against them, and the same for the dispensational rapture. The test of whether you have understood a view, the study says, is whether you can argue for it, not just against it. This is not a debate where one side wins on points. It is a discipline of honoring the people who read the same Bible and reached a different conclusion.

faq.q: Is it really okay for Christians to disagree about the end times?
faq.a: Yes, on the timeline, and the history of the church settles it. The early church did not put the millennium or the rapture in the creeds. It confessed that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and left the precise order of events open. Augustine, Aquinas, Luther, and Calvin read the thousand years symbolically, important early voices expected a literal earthly reign, and serious modern scholars defend each of the major positions, all of them loving Scripture and reading it closely. So disagreement about the shape and sequence of the end is not a test of who truly belongs to Christ, and a church that makes it one is adding a boundary God did not draw. What is not open for disagreement is the center, that Christ has come and is coming, that the dead will be raised, that the world will be made right. Open hands on the timeline, the study says. Closed fist on the center.

faq.q: Is the rapture in the Bible?
faq.a: The word rapture comes from the Latin for the catching-up that Paul describes in 1 Thessalonians 4, where the dead in Christ rise and the living are caught up to meet the Lord in the air, so a catching-up is certainly in the text. The contested question is what it describes. Dispensational premillennialism, the Left Behind framework developed by Darby and spread by the Scofield Bible, reads it as a secret removal of the church before a seven-year tribulation, and the study states that view at full strength, with its real scriptural anchors and its best modern defenders. But historic premillennialists and amillennialists read the same passage as the church going out to welcome the returning King at his single, public, loud coming, and they note that the two-stage secret-then-visible structure emerges clearly only in the 1800s. The study does not tell you which reading is right. It shows you that a real, bodily gathering to meet Christ is in the text, and that whether it is secret and pretribulational is genuinely contested among faithful readers.

faq.q: If date-setting has always been wrong, why study the end times at all?
faq.a: Because the point was never to set a date, and the study says so from the first session. Jesus himself said no one knows the day or the hour, not even the Son, and the disciples were told it was not for them to know the times the Father had fixed. Every confident prediction in two thousand years of church history, from the Montanists to William Miller to the chart-makers of the last century, has been wrong, and that record is a warning the study takes seriously. But refusing to set dates is not the same as ignoring the Christian hope. We study the end times the way the first readers of Revelation did, not to crack a code but to be steadied, to learn that the slaughtered Lamb is on the throne, to long rightly for the King who is coming, and to live faithfully in the meantime. The cure for bad end-times speculation is not silence about the last things. It is reading them rightly.

faq.q: What is the already and not yet, and why does the study say it is the center?
faq.a: It is the New Testament's way of describing the time we live in. The kingdom of God is already here, because in Jesus it has genuinely broken into history, the King has come, the Spirit is poured out, the decisive victory is won at the cross and the empty tomb. And the kingdom is not yet here in full, because the world is plainly not yet made right, sin and death and grief still operate, and we pray your kingdom come precisely because it has not fully come. Every faithful view of the end, whatever it says about the millennium, stands on this shared ground, which is why the study calls it the center. George Eldon Ladd and N.T. Wright gave it its modern shape. Living in the already and not yet means working as if the kingdom matters now, because it does, and waiting as people who know it is God's to finish, which guards against both fleeing the world and frantically trying to build heaven ourselves.

faq.q: Is the Christian hope that our souls go to heaven when we die?
faq.a: That is half of it, and the smaller half, and the study works hard to recover the larger one. It is true and comforting that at death the believer goes to be with Christ, consciously and joyfully, which Paul calls far better, and the grieving must never be denied that comfort. But being with Christ at death is the intermediate state, the waiting, not the final hope. The Bible ends not with souls floating up to heaven but with resurrection, the body raised, and new creation, the new Jerusalem coming down to earth, God dwelling with his people on a renewed world, every tear wiped away and death itself dead. N.T. Wright has pressed this on the church, that the goal is not us going up to heaven but heaven coming down. The hope is larger and more physical than the popular picture, not smaller, the world made right rather than abandoned, and the study insists that is better news, not worse.

faq.q: Does the study take the medical, I mean the historical and scholarly, dimension seriously, or is it just opinion?
faq.a: It is anchored in serious scholarship throughout, named openly so you can read further. George Eldon Ladd and N.T. Wright stand behind the already and not yet and the new-creation hope. Anthony Hoekema in The Bible and the Future, Kim Riddlebarger, and Sam Storms represent amillennialism. Loraine Boettner defends postmillennialism. Craig Blaising represents thoughtful modern dispensationalism. The history is handled honestly too, the second-century chiliasts, Augustine's symbolic reading that shaped the church for centuries, the rise of postmillennialism in the missionary era, and the nineteenth-century origin of the dispensational system through Darby and the Scofield Bible. The study does not hide where ideas came from, and it does not weaponize their origins either, insisting that the age of an idea does not by itself prove it true or false. You are getting fairly stated positions with real defenders, not the leader's private opinions dressed up as the obvious faith.

faq.q: I was taught the rapture my whole life. Is this study going to tell me I was wrong?
faq.a: No. It is going to tell you that you were taught one serious reading among several, and ask you to understand the others before you decide. The dispensational rapture is held by millions, built by sincere and capable people, and anchored in real texts, and the study states it at full strength rather than mocking it, which the Left Behind brand can tempt people to do. What the study will gently challenge is not your view itself but the assumption, if you hold it, that the rapture is simply the plain and obvious reading any honest believer would reach, when in fact the entire church, including its most literal interpreters, read these texts differently for eighteen centuries. You are welcome to keep your view if the text persuades you. The study only asks you to hold it as a reading among faithful readings, not as the password to true faith, and to extend to those who differ the same honor you would want.

faq.q: Why does the study refuse to end with a chart or a clear timeline?
faq.a: Because the charts were part of the problem, and because the actual hope is too large to diagram. End-times charts give the comforting feeling of mastery, of having the future pinned down and labeled, and that feeling is exactly the impulse that has produced two thousand years of failed predictions and divided churches. More than that, the Christian hope at its fullest, the dead raised, the world made right, God come down to dwell with his people, every grave giving back what it took, is not a sequence to be mapped but a weight to be carried and a longing to be felt. The final session ends deliberately at the edge of that hope rather than in the middle of a diagram, because the point of the whole study was never to settle the order of events. It was to make people who hold the Christian hope with both conviction and humility, who long for the King, and who have stopped using the end of the world as a chart to argue over.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have a strong view of my own?
faq.a: Your view is not a disqualification, but it is something to manage carefully. Most leaders have a position, and that is fine. The danger is leading in a way that recruits the room to your camp, because the fastest way to break this study is for the group to figure out which side the facilitator is on and start performing agreement to belong. So in the room, keep your own conviction quiet enough that no one feels that pressure. If a member asks privately where you land, you may tell them gently, as one reading among several, then turn them straight back to the text and the other views. Your real job is to enforce the steelman rule, to make the room state each view fairly before critiquing it, to slow down anyone rushing to attack a straw man, and to guard the center while keeping the timeline open. Deal with your own certainty before session one, because a leader who walks in with the answers will turn this study into the very division it exists to prevent.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is not the whole idea of the world being made right just wishful thinking?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study takes it seriously because Bell once made exactly that argument as an atheist, that the Christian hope was a fairy tale for people too afraid to face that death is the end. The study grants that a hope this large could be wishful thinking, and that longing for the world to be made right does not by itself prove it will be. But it then puts the actual Christian claim on the table, which is not a vague hope but a specific historical assertion, that one man already rose bodily from the dead as the firstfruits, the first instance of the renewal promised for everything else. The Christian hope is not built on how badly we want death to lose. It is built on the claim that death already lost, once, and that the empty tomb is the seed of a renewed creation. You can examine that claim, weigh the evidence, decide whether it holds. The study does not ask you to want it true. It asks you to consider whether it is.

timeline.event: In the crisis under Antiochus the Fourth, the visions of Daniel give the people of God a language of beasts and kingdoms and a God who outlasts every empire, founding the apocalyptic imagery that Revelation will later draw upon.

Jesus announces that the kingdom of God has come near and is in the midst of his hearers, and also teaches them to pray for the kingdom to come, planting the already and not yet at the heart of Christian hope, and he refuses to name the day or hour of the end.

Paul writes to the Thessalonians to comfort those grieving believers who have died, describing the dead in Christ rising and the living being caught up to meet the Lord, the passage from which the later idea of the rapture is drawn.

John writes the Revelation to seven churches in Asia Minor under Roman pressure, a work of apocalyptic literature meant to steady the persecuted with the vision that the slaughtered Lamb reigns and Rome does not, ending with a new heaven and new earth.

Montanus and his followers in Phrygia expect the imminent descent of the New Jerusalem and a new age of the Spirit, an early instance of fervent end-times expectation that did not come to pass, beginning the long record of failed prediction.

A form of premillennial expectation, often called chiliasm, is held by some early Christian writers who look for a literal earthly reign of Christ, though it is contested and never the universal view of the early church.

Augustine, in The City of God, sets out the symbolic reading of the thousand years as the present age of the church, the view that becomes amillennialism and shapes Western Christianity, Catholic and later Protestant, for more than a thousand years.

The magisterial Reformers, Luther and Calvin among them, retain the broadly Augustinian symbolic reading of the millennium, so that the recovery of the gospel does not bring with it a literal earthly reign or a rapture scheme.

Postmillennial hope flowers in the era of awakening and expanding missions, as confidence in the gospel's power to transform the world makes the expectation of a coming golden age feel compelling to many serious believers.

John Nelson Darby, among the early Plymouth Brethren in Britain and Ireland, develops dispensationalism, with its sharp Israel-church distinction and its pretribulation rapture, a genuine theological innovation rather than a recovery of ancient teaching.

William Miller's followers, having calculated the return of Christ for October 22, gather and wait, and the day passes into what they themselves call the Great Disappointment, the most famous failed prediction in American religious history.

The Scofield Reference Bible is published, embedding Darby's dispensational framework in study notes printed alongside the biblical text, spreading the system across American Christianity until many absorb it as though it were Scripture itself.

George Eldon Ladd publishes work advancing the already and not yet and a careful historic premillennialism distinct from dispensationalism, recovering the inaugurated kingdom for evangelical scholarship and refusing the secret two-stage coming.

Anthony Hoekema publishes The Bible and the Future, a careful and influential modern statement of amillennialism and the new-creation hope, giving the symbolic reading of the millennium a clear contemporary voice.

N.T. Wright publishes Surprised by Hope, pressing on the whole church that the Christian hope is not souls going up to heaven but resurrection and the renewal of all creation, heaven coming down to a healed earth.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here, because this is a subject people usually either avoid or fight about, and you showed up to do neither. Before we start, three things. First, this study has one rule above all others. We are going to hold open hands on the timeline and a closed fist on the center. That means we will disagree, honestly and freely, about the order and shape of the end, because faithful Christians have for two thousand years, and we will not disagree about what the whole church confesses, that Christ has come, that he will come again, that the dead will be raised, and that the world will be made right. Second, we are going to state every view at its strongest before anyone argues against it. The test of whether you understand a position is whether you can argue for it, not just against it, so if you find yourself wanting to knock a view down, first make yourself state it so well that someone who holds it would nod. Third, the writer does not stand above this, and neither do I. He came to faith from atheism thinking the whole thing was a fairy tale, and he has done his own date-math in the dark and used the end as an escape from a world he was meant to love. We are inside this together. Tonight we are looking at this: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before anyone says a word. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have stated the views fairly and held them at their strongest. Now let us bring it home, off the chart and into the way we actually live and hope and love the people across the table from us, because that is where this either matters or it does not.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop here, and notice we are stopping without a tidy chart, on purpose, because the point was never to pin down the order of events. Take the center out of this room with you this week, that Christ has come and is coming and will make the world right, and hold it heavier than any timeline. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection on your own. And if you came in certain that your view was the only faithful one, carry out a little more room for the brother and sister who read it differently, because that charity is part of the hope too. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for the honesty and the humility it took to be in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the one rule, open hands on the timeline and closed fist on the center, and establish the steelman discipline before any content.
Week 2: Session 1, Reading the End Rightly, the genre of apocalyptic and the long record of failed prediction.
Week 3: Session 2, part one, premillennialism and postmillennialism each steelmanned at full strength.
Week 4: Session 2, part two, amillennialism steelmanned, then the posture of holding all three with open hands.
Week 5: Session 3, Rapture, Tribulation, and the Dispensational Debate, the dispensational case at full strength.
Week 6: Session 3 continued, the historic-premillennial and amillennial alternatives, and what is and is not at stake.
Week 7: Session 4, Already and Not Yet, the shared center and the dangers of escapism and date-setting.
Week 8: Session 5, The New Creation, resurrection and renewed earth, ending at the edge of the hope rather than with a chart.

plan: Week 1: Session 1, Reading the End Rightly, with the steelman rule and the center established up front.
Week 2: Session 2, The Millennium, the Three Readings, all three steelmanned.
Week 3: Sessions 3 and 4 together, the rapture debate and the already and not yet that all the views share.
Week 4: Session 5, The New Creation, plus a short integration close at the edge of the resurrection hope.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Hope: Rethinking Heaven, the Resurrection, and the Mission of the Church
bibliography.author: N.T. Wright
bibliography.note: The central modern recovery of the new-creation hope, that the goal is not souls going up to heaven but heaven coming down to a renewed earth. The spine of session 5.

bibliography.title: The Presence of the Future and A Theology of the New Testament
bibliography.author: George Eldon Ladd
bibliography.note: The classic evangelical statement of the already and not yet and of a careful historic premillennialism distinct from dispensationalism. Anchors sessions 3 and 4. Leader to confirm specific claims before pressing them as settled.

bibliography.title: The Bible and the Future
bibliography.author: Anthony A. Hoekema
bibliography.note: A careful and influential statement of amillennialism and the new-creation hope, the best single defense of the symbolic reading of the millennium. Essential for steelmanning amillennialism in session 2.

bibliography.title: A Case for Amillennialism: Understanding the End Times
bibliography.author: Kim Riddlebarger
bibliography.note: A clear and accessible modern defense of amillennialism, useful for stating that view at full strength. Supports session 2. Leader to confirm specifics before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: Kingdom Come: The Amillennial Alternative
bibliography.author: Sam Storms
bibliography.note: A vigorous and detailed contemporary case for amillennialism. Offered as an able advocate for the symbolic reading in session 2, to be presented fairly alongside the other views.

bibliography.title: The Millennium: A Postmillennial Study, and broader writing on eschatology
bibliography.author: Loraine Boettner
bibliography.note: A vigorous defense of postmillennialism and the confidence that the gospel will transform the world before Christ returns. The best advocate to steelman the postmillennial view in session 2. Leader to confirm specifics.

bibliography.title: Progressive Dispensationalism
bibliography.author: Craig A. Blaising and Darrell L. Bock
bibliography.note: A thoughtful, careful modern refinement of dispensational premillennialism by serious scholars, useful for stating the dispensational case at full strength rather than in caricature. Essential for session 3.

bibliography.title: The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views
bibliography.author: Robert G. Clouse, editor
bibliography.note: A classic point-counterpoint volume in which advocates of each major view state and defend their own position, an ideal resource for the study's steelman method across sessions 2 and 3.

bibliography.title: Four Views on the Book of Revelation
bibliography.author: C. Marvin Pate, editor
bibliography.note: Presents the major approaches to reading Revelation side by side, helpful for session 1 on genre and for understanding why the same text yields different end-times schemes.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The source of the symbolic reading of the thousand years as the present church age that shaped Western Christianity for over a millennium. Essential historical background for the amillennial view in session 2.

bibliography.title: The Last Things: Resurrection, Judgment, Glory
bibliography.author: George Eldon Ladd
bibliography.note: A short, accessible treatment of the Christian hope oriented around resurrection and new creation. Supports sessions 4 and 5. Leader to confirm before stating its arguments as the study's position.

bibliography.title: Reversed Thunder: The Revelation of John and the Praying Imagination
bibliography.author: Eugene H. Peterson
bibliography.note: A pastoral reading of Revelation that recovers its purpose as worship and formation rather than prediction, a good corrective for session 1's work on genre. Offered as a voice that reads the book devotionally rather than as a code.

The Bible and the Future, Anthony Hoekema, for those who want the fullest careful statement of amillennialism and the symbolic reading of the thousand years.
Progressive Dispensationalism, Blaising and Bock, for readers who want to understand the dispensational view in its most thoughtful modern form rather than through the popular novels.
Reversed Thunder, Eugene Peterson, for anyone who wants to read Revelation as worship and formation rather than as a code to crack, a companion to the genre work of session 1.

glossary.definition: The study of the last things, the doctrine of how the story ends, including death, resurrection, judgment, the return of Christ, and the new creation. The study treats its contested parts with open hands and its central confession with a closed fist.

A genre of writing, including Daniel and Revelation, born among the persecuted people of God, dense with symbol, number, beast, and vision, written to steady the faithful with the assurance that God reigns and the oppressor will fall. It is not a coded calendar or a newspaper of the future.

Latin for a thousand years, the period mentioned in Revelation 20 and read three ways by the church, as a future earthly reign after Christ returns, as a golden age before he returns, or as the present church age understood symbolically.

The reading that Christ returns before, pre, a thousand-year reign on earth, taking the sequence of Revelation 19 and 20 as consecutive. Held in a historic form by George Eldon Ladd and in a dispensational form by Darby and his heirs.

The reading that the gospel will so advance through history that the world enters a long golden age, after which, post, Christ returns. It takes the parables of leaven and mustard seed and the promise that the knowledge of the Lord will fill the earth as a confidence in the gospel's power in history. Defended by Loraine Boettner.

The reading that the thousand years is symbolic, the present age between Christ's two comings, in which he reigns from heaven and Satan is bound from deceiving the nations. Held by Augustine and the Reformers and defended today by Hoekema, Riddlebarger, and Storms.

A system developed by John Nelson Darby in the 1800s and spread by the Scofield Bible, dividing history into distinct ages and keeping a sharp distinction between Israel and the church, from which follows its signature pretribulation rapture.

From the Latin for the catching-up Paul describes in 1 Thessalonians 4, the gathering of believers to meet the returning Lord. Whether it is a secret event before a tribulation or the church welcoming Christ at his single, public coming is contested among faithful readers.

A period of intense trouble before the end. Dispensationalism reads a specific future seven-year tribulation from which the church is removed, while other views read the tribulation language as describing the pressure the church has lived under throughout the present age.

The New Testament's description of the present time, in which the kingdom of God has already broken in through Christ yet has not yet fully come. The shared center of every faithful view of the end, given modern shape by George Eldon Ladd and N.T. Wright.

The conviction that the kingdom of God has genuinely begun in Jesus, decisively launched at the cross and resurrection, even as it awaits its consummation at his return. The same reality as the already and not yet, named from the side of the already.

The Bible's final hope, the renewal rather than destruction of the world, a new heaven and new earth joined when the city of God descends, God dwelling with his people, every tear wiped away and death itself abolished. The world made right, not abandoned.

The creedal hope that the dead will be raised bodily, not merely that souls survive death, patterned on the bodily resurrection of Jesus as the firstfruits, affirming that the physical body and the material world are part of what God will redeem.

The condition of believers between death and the resurrection, consciously with Christ, which Paul calls far better. Real and comforting, but not the final hope, which is the resurrection of the body and the renewed creation.
